papers.title: On coherence of enveloping algebras of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27824v1

summary.one_liner: The paper studies when universal enveloping algebras of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras are coherent, showing a sharp nilpotency criterion for loop algebras, non-coherence for a class of simple graded Lie algebras, and coherence results for related graded and filtered rings.
summary.plain: This paper is about a property called "coherence" for a certain kind of algebraic structure built from symmetry rules (Lie algebras). Coherence roughly means that certain systems of equations built from these structures behave nicely, so that their solutions are finitely describable. The authors determine exactly when this holds for loop algebras, show it fails for a broad family of simple infinite-dimensional algebras, and prove some positive results for related rings.
summary.why: The text gives the main results but not their wider consequences. It is a specialist result in ring theory, and it sits alongside earlier work on whether these algebras are Noetherian (every chain of ideals stabilizes), so it likely matters mainly to researchers in that area.
summary.background:
- Lie algebra: an algebra of infinitesimal symmetries, with a bracket operation.
- Universal enveloping algebra U(g): a ring built from a Lie algebra g that encodes its structure.
- Infinite-dimensional: the algebra has infinitely many independent directions, unlike finite-dimensional matrix Lie algebras.
- Loop algebra: functions from a circle (or Laurent polynomials) with values in a finite-dimensional Lie algebra h.
- Nilpotent: repeated brackets eventually vanish.
- Coherent ring: finitely generated one-sided ideals are finitely presented, a finiteness condition weaker than Noetherian.
- Graded and filtered rings: rings split into pieces by degree, or equipped with a nested sequence of subspaces; the Rees ring is a standard way to pass between the two.
- Witt algebra: the Lie algebra of derivations of Laurent polynomials, a standard example of an infinite-dimensional simple Lie algebra.

papers.abstract: We investigate when the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{g})$ of an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ is coherent. We show that if $\mathfrak{g}$ is the loop algebra of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{h}$ then $U(\mathfrak{g})$ is coherent exactly when $\mathfrak{h}$ is nilpotent. As a consequence, we show that $U(\mathfrak{g})$ is not coherent if $\mathfrak{g}$ is complex, simple, $\mathbb{Z}$-graded, of polynomially bounded growth, and not isomorphic to the Witt algebra $W = \mathrm{Der} \mathbb{C}[t,t^{-1}]$ or its one-sided version. We also demonstrate that the homomorphic image of $U(W)$ used to prove non-Noetherianity of $U(W)$ in previous work of the first author and Walton is not coherent. On the other hand, we establish that two closely related connected graded rings are graded coherent. Finally, we prove that any exhaustively filtered ring is coherent if its Rees ring is graded coherent.

papers.title: Large orbits of $p$-groups on conjugacy classes of arbitrary finite groups
papers.label: arXiv:2611.27916v1

summary.one_liner: The paper removes the solvability assumption from a result that, for a p-group acting coprimely and faithfully on a finite group H, finds a conjugacy class (or irreducible character) whose stabilizer in P has order at most |P|^{1/2}, with the bound shown to be sharp, using the classification of finite simple groups and a new lemma on quasiprimitive linear actions of p-nilpotent groups.
summary.plain: This paper is about symmetries of finite group structures: a small group of symmetries (a "p-group," a group whose size is a power of a prime p) acts on another finite group, and the question is how many of those symmetries can leave some piece of the structure unchanged. A previous result handled the case where the group is solvable, a technical class of groups that can be built up step by step from simple pieces; this paper drops that restriction. The authors show the same bound holds in general, with a proof that relies on the classification of finite simple groups.
summary.why: The result gives a guaranteed size limit on how much of a symmetry group can fix a piece of structure, and the authors show the limit is sharp by giving new examples with nonsolvable groups where it is attained. The text does not say what wider applications it has, so its broader significance beyond this area is unclear to me.
summary.background:
- Finite group: a group with finitely many elements, such as the symmetries of a finite set.
- Group action: a way a group's elements permute or transform another object.
- p-group: a group whose number of elements is a power of a prime p.
- Coprime action: the acting group's order shares no prime factor with the acted-on group's order.
- Stabilizer: the set of symmetries that leave a given element (or class, or character) unchanged; its order is how many such symmetries there are.
- Conjugacy class and irreducible character: standard objects describing the internal structure of a finite group.
- Solvable group: a group that can be built from abelian (commutative) pieces in layers; nonsolvable groups are the more complex case.
- Classification of finite simple groups: a large, known list of the basic building blocks of finite groups, used as a deep tool in the proof.

papers.abstract: Let $P$ be a $p$-group that acts faithfully and coprimely on a finite group $H$. In a previous paper it was shown that if $H$ is solvable, then there exists a conjugacy class $c$ of $H$ whose stabilizer in $P$ has order at most $|P|^{1/2}$, and that this bound is best possible. In this paper we remove the hypothesis that $H$ is solvable. As a consequence, there always exists an irreducible character of $H$ whose inertia group in $P$ has order at most $|P|^{1/2}$. The proof depends on the classification of finite simple groups. Its main new ingredient is a result on quasiprimitive linear actions of $p$-nilpotent groups which shows that the elements acting as field automorphisms can be ignored when one looks for vectors with small stabilizers. We also present a new family of examples, with nonsolvable $H$, in which the bound is attained.
